title: Hands-on Exercise 1
text: This exercise follows Chapters 1 and 2 of R for Geospatial Data Science and Analytics. Part 1 prepares and analyses spatial data. Part 2 turns population data into choropleth maps.

title: Hands-on Exercise 1
text:
Part 1: Geospatial data wrangling

1.1 Data acquisition
The exercise uses four datasets. The original Master Plan 2014 “Web” file is no longer available from its collection, so the current official “No Sea” GeoJSON is used instead. This changes the import format, but not the analysis.



Dataset
Format used
Source




Master Plan 2014 Subzone Boundary (No Sea)
GeoJSON polygon
URA via data.gov.sg


Pre-Schools Location
GeoJSON point
ECDA via data.gov.sg


Cycling Path Network
GeoJSON line
LTA via data.gov.sg


Singapore Airbnb listings, 29 June 2026
CSV table
Inside Airbnb



The files are stored in separate geospatial and aspatial folders.
data/
├── geospatial/
│   ├── MasterPlan2014SubzoneBoundaryNoSea.geojson
│   ├── MasterPlan2019SubzoneBoundaryNoSea.geojson
│   ├── PreSchoolsLocation.geojson
│   └── CyclingPathNetwork.geojson
└── aspatial/
    ├── listings.csv
    └── respopagesextod2024.csv


1.2 Getting started
sf handles vector data, while packages in tidyverse import, transform and visualise the data. tmap is used in Part 2.

pacman::p_load(sf, tidyverse, tmap, classInt, knitr)

theme_set(theme_minimal(base_size = 12))



1.3 Importing geospatial data

Importing the polygon layer
st_read() imports the Master Plan 2014 subzone boundaries as a simple feature data frame named mpsz.

mpsz <- st_read(
  "data/geospatial/MasterPlan2014SubzoneBoundaryNoSea.geojson"
)

1.5 Plotting geospatial data
A quick geometry plot checks the shape and extent of the subzone layer.

plot(
  st_geometry(mpsz),
  col = "#e7ece9",
  border = "white",
  main = "Master Plan 2014 subzones"
)








An attribute plot colours the polygons by planning area.

plot(
  mpsz["PLN_AREA_N"],
  key.pos = 4,
  main = "Singapore planning areas"
)










1.6 Working with projection
The current GeoJSON files are correctly labelled WGS 84 (EPSG:4326). They must be transformed to Singapore SVY21 (EPSG:3414) before calculating distances or areas.

tibble(
  layer = c("Subzones", "Cycling paths", "Pre-schools"),
  crs = c(
    st_crs(mpsz)$Name,
    st_crs(cyclingpath)$Name,
    st_crs(preschool)$Name
  )
) |>
  kable()




layer
crs




Subzones
WGS 84


Cycling paths
WGS 84


Pre-schools
WGS 84





st_transform() recalculates the coordinates in the target CRS. st_set_crs() is not used because the source CRS is already correct; relabelling the coordinates would put the features in the wrong place.

mpsz <- st_transform(mpsz, 3414)
cyclingpath <- st_transform(cyclingpath, 3414)
preschool <- st_transform(preschool, 3414)

tibble(
  layer = c("Subzones", "Cycling paths", "Pre-schools"),
  epsg = c(
    st_crs(mpsz)$epsg,
    st_crs(cyclingpath)$epsg,
    st_crs(preschool)$epsg
  )
) |>
  kable()




layer
epsg




Subzones
3414


Cycling paths
3414


Pre-schools
3414





The transformed layers now share the same projected coordinate system and can be overlaid.

ggplot() +
  geom_sf(data = mpsz, fill = "#edf1ef", colour = "white", linewidth = 0.15) +
  geom_sf(data = preschool, colour = "#d85b3f", size = 0.25, alpha = 0.65) +
  coord_sf(datum = NA) +
  labs(
    title = "Pre-school locations",
    subtitle = "Master Plan 2014 subzones"
  ) +
  theme_void()

Importing the Airbnb table
read_csv() imports the latest Singapore listings as a tibble.

listings <- read_csv(
  "data/aspatial/listings.csv",
  show_col_types = FALSE
)

Creating a simple feature data frame
Longitude and latitude are WGS 84 coordinates. st_as_sf() creates point geometry, and st_transform() converts the result to SVY21.

  drop_na(longitude, latitude) |>
  st_as_sf(
    coords = c("longitude", "latitude"),
    crs = 4326

  st_transform(3414)

1.8 Geoprocessing with sf

Use case 1: land around cycling paths
A five-metre buffer marks the land within five metres of each cycling path segment.

buffer_cycling <- st_buffer(
  cyclingpath,
  dist = 5,
  nQuadSegs = 30
)


ggplot() +
  geom_sf(data = mpsz, fill = "#f4f5f2", colour = "white", linewidth = 0.1) +
  geom_sf(data = buffer_cycling, fill = "#d85b3f", colour = NA, alpha = 0.75) +
  coord_sf(datum = NA) +
  labs(title = "Five-metre cycling path buffer") +
  theme_void()








Summing the individual polygon areas gives the combined segment-level estimate.

buffer_area_ha <- sum(st_area(buffer_cycling)) |>
  units::set_units(ha)

tibble(
  measure = "Sum of individual 5 m buffers",
  area_hectares = round(as.numeric(buffer_area_ha), 2)
) |>
  kable()




measure
area_hectares




Sum of individual 5 m buffers
498.97





The estimate is 498.97 hectares. Overlapping buffers are counted more than once, so this is a segment-level total rather than a dissolved land footprint.


Use case 2: number of pre-schools by subzone
st_intersects() identifies which pre-school points fall inside each subzone. lengths() converts the list of matches into a count.

mpsz$PreSch_count <- lengths(
  st_intersects(mpsz, preschool)
)

mpsz |>
  st_drop_geometry() |>
  select(SUBZONE_N, PLN_AREA_N, PreSch_count) |>
  arrange(desc(PreSch_count)) |>
  slice_head(n = 10) |>
  kable(
    col.names = c("Subzone", "Planning area", "Pre-schools"),
    caption = "Ten subzones with the most pre-schools"
  )

1.9 Exploratory data analysis

Deriving area and density
Area is converted from square metres to square kilometres. Dividing the facility count by area gives pre-school density.

mpsz <- mpsz |>
  mutate(
    Area_km2 = as.numeric(units::set_units(st_area(geometry), km^2)),
    PreSch_density = PreSch_count / Area_km2
  )

mpsz |>
  st_drop_geometry() |>
  select(SUBZONE_N, PLN_AREA_N, PreSch_count, Area_km2, PreSch_density) |>
  arrange(desc(PreSch_density)) |>
  slice_head(n = 10) |>
  mutate(
    Area_km2 = round(Area_km2, 2),
    PreSch_density = round(PreSch_density, 2)
  ) |>
  kable(
    col.names = c("Subzone", "Planning area", "Count", "Area (km²)", "Density per km²"),

Histogram

  geom_histogram(binwidth = 5, boundary = 0, colour = "white", fill = "#39735f") +

  geom_point(colour = "#d85b3f", alpha = 0.65) +

title: Hands-on Exercise 1
text:
Part 2: Choropleth mapping

2.1 Getting started
Part 2 uses tmap for thematic mapping. Static plot mode keeps the maps suitable for the report page.

tmap_mode("plot")



2.2 Importing data

Importing Master Plan 2019 subzones

Importing resident population data
The 2024 SingStat data is stored as a CSV with planning area, subzone, age group, sex, population and year fields.

  "data/aspatial/respopagesextod2024.csv",
  na = c("na", "-", ""),

2.3 Preparing the population table
The dependency ratio compares young and aged residents with the economically active age group.
\[
\text{Dependency ratio} =
\frac{\text{Young} + \text{Aged}}
{\text{Economically active}}
\]

Young: ages 0–24
Economically active: ages 25–64
Aged: ages 65 and above

The data is aggregated across sex and reshaped from age-group rows to columns.

popdata2024 <- popdata |>
  filter(PA != "Total", SZ != "Total", AG != "Total") |>
  group_by(PA, SZ, AG) |>
  summarise(POP = sum(Pop, na.rm = TRUE), .groups = "drop") |>
  pivot_wider(names_from = AG, values_from = POP, values_fill = 0) |>
  mutate(
    YOUNG = rowSums(across(c(
      `0 - 4`, `5 - 9`, `10 - 14`, `15 - 19`, `20 - 24`
    ))),
    `ECONOMY ACTIVE` = rowSums(across(c(
      `25 - 29`, `30 - 34`, `35 - 39`, `40 - 44`,
      `45 - 49`, `50 - 54`, `55 - 59`, `60 - 64`
    ))),
    AGED = rowSums(across(c(
      `65 - 69`, `70 - 74`, `75 - 79`, `80 - 84`,
      `85 - 89`, `90 & Over`
    ))),
    TOTAL = YOUNG + `ECONOMY ACTIVE` + AGED,
    DEPENDENCY = (YOUNG + AGED) / `ECONOMY ACTIVE`
  ) |>
  mutate(across(c(PA, SZ), str_to_upper)) |>
  filter(`ECONOMY ACTIVE` > 0) |>
  select(PA, SZ, YOUNG, `ECONOMY ACTIVE`, AGED, TOTAL, DEPENDENCY)

popdata2024 |>
  arrange(desc(DEPENDENCY)) |>
  slice_head(n = 10) |>

    col.names = c(
      "Planning area", "Subzone", "Young", "Economically active",
      "Aged", "Total", "Dependency ratio"
    ),
    caption = "Highest calculated dependency ratios"
  )

2.4 Joining attributes to subzones
The spatial layer stays on the left of left_join(), so the result remains an sf object. Upper-case subzone names provide the common key.

mpsz_pop2024 <- mpsz19 |>
  mutate(SUBZONE_N = str_to_upper(SUBZONE_N)) |>
  left_join(
    popdata2024,
    by = c("SUBZONE_N" = "SZ")
  )

join_check <- mpsz_pop2024 |>
  st_drop_geometry() |>
  summarise(
    subzones = n(),
    matched = sum(!is.na(DEPENDENCY)),
    unmatched = sum(is.na(DEPENDENCY))
  )

join_check |>
  kable(caption = "Population-to-boundary join check")


Population-to-boundary join check


subzones
matched
unmatched




332

94





The join matches 238 of 332 subzones. The remaining 94 polygons have no dependency value, mainly because they have no resident population record or use a different subzone label.

dir.create("data/rds", showWarnings = FALSE)
write_rds(mpsz_pop2024, "data/rds/mpsz_pop2024.rds")



2.5 Quick choropleth map
qtm() provides a fast first view of the dependency ratio.

qtm(
  shp = mpsz_pop2024,
  fill = "DEPENDENCY",
  title = "Dependency ratio by subzone"
)










2.6 Building a choropleth with tmap
tm_shape() defines the spatial object. tm_polygons() maps the dependency ratio to polygon fill, while tm_borders() separates neighbouring subzones.

tm_shape(mpsz_pop2024) +
  tm_polygons(
    fill = "DEPENDENCY",
    fill.legend = tm_legend(title = "Dependency ratio")
  ) +
  tm_borders(col = "white", lwd = 0.4) +
  tm_title("Dependency ratio by planning subzone")










2.7 Comparing classification methods
The class method changes which subzones appear similar. Equal intervals use equally sized numeric ranges; quantiles place similar numbers of subzones in each class; Jenks natural breaks follow clusters in the data.

map_equal <- tm_shape(mpsz_pop2024) +
  tm_polygons(
    fill = "DEPENDENCY",
    fill.scale = tm_scale_intervals(
      style = "equal", n = 5, values = "brewer.greens"
    ),
    fill.legend = tm_legend(title = "Equal")
  ) +
  tm_borders(col = "white", lwd = 0.3)

map_quantile <- tm_shape(mpsz_pop2024) +
  tm_polygons(
    fill = "DEPENDENCY",
    fill.scale = tm_scale_intervals(
      style = "quantile", n = 5, values = "brewer.greens"
    ),
    fill.legend = tm_legend(title = "Quantile")
  ) +
  tm_borders(col = "white", lwd = 0.3)

map_jenks <- tm_shape(mpsz_pop2024) +
  tm_polygons(
    fill = "DEPENDENCY",
    fill.scale = tm_scale_intervals(
      style = "jenks", n = 5, values = "brewer.greens"
    ),
    fill.legend = tm_legend(title = "Jenks")
  ) +
  tm_borders(col = "white", lwd = 0.3)

tmap_arrange(map_equal, map_quantile, map_jenks, ncol = 3)








The equal-interval map is dominated by the low classes because a few large ratios stretch the range. Quantiles provide the clearest island-wide comparison, while Jenks highlights breaks in the observed distribution.

Comparing the number of classes
The maps below hold the quantile method constant and vary the number of classes.

quantile_map <- function(classes) {
  tm_shape(mpsz_pop2024) +
    tm_polygons(
      fill = "DEPENDENCY",
      fill.scale = tm_scale_intervals(
        style = "quantile",
        n = classes,
        values = "brewer.greens"
      ),
      fill.legend = tm_legend(title = paste(classes, "classes"))
    ) +
    tm_borders(col = "white", lwd = 0.25)
}

tmap_arrange(
  quantile_map(2),
  quantile_map(6),
  quantile_map(10),
  quantile_map(20),
  ncol = 2
)








Two classes remove most local variation. Twenty classes add detail but make the legend and spatial pattern difficult to read. Five or six classes provide a clearer balance.



2.8 Custom breaks and colour
The summary below provides the basis for manual class breaks.

summary(mpsz_pop2024$DEPENDENCY)

   Min. 1st Qu.  Median    Mean 3rd Qu.    Max.     NAs 
 0.0000  0.6730  0.7324  0.7595  0.8109 10.0000      94 


The custom map uses breaks at 0.60, 0.70, 0.80 and 0.90, with the final class extending to the observed maximum.

dependency_max <- max(mpsz_pop2024$DEPENDENCY, na.rm = TRUE)

tm_shape(mpsz_pop2024) +
  tm_polygons(
    fill = "DEPENDENCY",
    fill.scale = tm_scale_intervals(
      breaks = c(0, 0.60, 0.70, 0.80, 0.90, dependency_max),
      values = "brewer.greens"
    ),
    fill.legend = tm_legend(title = "Dependency ratio")
  ) +
  tm_borders(col = "white", lwd = 0.3)








A sequential green palette suits an ordered ratio: darker shades indicate higher values. Reversing the palette would make low values appear visually dominant, so the original direction is retained.


2.9 Final cartographic map
The final map uses six quantile classes, a concise title, border lines, a compass, a scale bar and a source note.

final_map <- tm_shape(mpsz_pop2024) +
  tm_polygons(
    fill = "DEPENDENCY",
    fill.scale = tm_scale_intervals(
      style = "quantile",
      n = 6,
      values = "brewer.greens"
    ),
    fill.legend = tm_legend(
      title = "Dependency ratio",
      position = tm_pos_in("left", "bottom")
    )
  ) +
  tm_borders(col = "white", lwd = 0.35) +
  tm_title("Dependency ratio by Singapore planning subzone, 2024") +
  tm_compass(type = "8star", position = tm_pos_in("right", "top")) +
  tm_scalebar(position = tm_pos_in("right", "bottom")) +
  tm_credits(
    "Sources: URA Master Plan 2019; Singapore Department of Statistics",
    position = tm_pos_out("left", "bottom")
  ) +
  tm_layout(frame = FALSE)

final_map








The map shows the ratio, not the absolute number of dependants. A high value indicates more young and older residents relative to ages 25–64; it does not by itself measure service demand or household burden.


2.10 Small multiple maps
Young and aged population totals are mapped separately with the same classification method.

young_map <- tm_shape(mpsz_pop2024) +
  tm_polygons(
    fill = "YOUNG",
    fill.scale = tm_scale_intervals(
      style = "quantile", n = 5, values = "brewer.blues"
    ),
    fill.legend = tm_legend(title = "Young residents")
  ) +
  tm_borders(col = "white", lwd = 0.3)

aged_map <- tm_shape(mpsz_pop2024) +
  tm_polygons(
    fill = "AGED",
    fill.scale = tm_scale_intervals(
      style = "quantile", n = 5, values = "brewer.oranges"
    ),
    fill.legend = tm_legend(title = "Aged residents")
  ) +
  tm_borders(col = "white", lwd = 0.3)

tmap_arrange(young_map, aged_map, ncol = 2)








The two maps separate population composition from the dependency ratio and make different concentrations visible.


2.11 Mapping a selected region
Filtering the sf object before mapping focuses the analysis on the Central Region.

central_region <- mpsz_pop2024 |>
  filter(REGION_N == "CENTRAL REGION")

tm_shape(central_region) +
  tm_polygons(
    fill = "DEPENDENCY",
    fill.scale = tm_scale_intervals(
      style = "quantile", n = 5, values = "brewer.greens"
    ),
    fill.legend = tm_legend(title = "Dependency ratio")
  ) +
  tm_borders(col = "white", lwd = 0.4) +
  tm_title("Central Region dependency ratio")










2.12 Interactive map
Plot mode is switched to view mode for an interactive map. Hovering and clicking reveal the subzone name and dependency ratio.

tmap_mode("view")

tm_shape(mpsz_pop2024) +
  tm_polygons(
    fill = "DEPENDENCY",
    fill.scale = tm_scale_intervals(
      style = "quantile", n = 6, values = "brewer.greens"
    ),
    fill.legend = tm_legend(title = "Dependency ratio"),
    id = "SUBZONE_N",
    popup.vars = c(
      "Subzone" = "SUBZONE_N",
      "Planning area" = "PLN_AREA_N",
      "Dependency ratio" = "DEPENDENCY"
    )
  ) +
  tm_borders(col = "white", lwd = 0.5) +
  tm_view(set_zoom_limits = c(10, 14))





tmap_mode("plot")

title: Hands-on Exercise 1
text:
Conclusion
The exercise shows that geospatial analysis depends on preparation before mapping. All layers must use a suitable CRS, spatial joins must be checked, and classification choices must be explained. The final map is therefore supported by the import checks, transformations and calculations shown above rather than presented as an isolated graphic.
